summaries.example: Maya offers to sell Leo her old bicycle for $40. Leo agrees, and both expect the deal to happen. If Maya breaks the agreement, the law may give Leo money for what he expected to receive. Philosophers ask whether this is because promises should be kept, because Leo might be harmed, because agreements help people cooperate, or because several reasons work together.
summaries.summary: A contract is a legally recognized agreement that changes what people may claim from one another and what they must do. The philosophy of contract law asks why these agreements should be enforced. One answer says the law protects the moral duty to keep promises. Another says it prevents harm when people reasonably rely on what they were told. A third says contracts help people coordinate, invest, and make exchanges that benefit everyone involved. A fourth focuses on the special relationship created when people join their choices in a shared project. A pluralist view says contract law may pursue several goals, even when those goals pull in different directions. The source also connects contracts with questions about clear language, free choice, intention, and fairness. These theories do not fit every legal rule perfectly, so the best explanation remains debated.
key_ideas: Contracts let people create legal duties by making and accepting agreements.
One theory says contracts are mainly about keeping promises.
Another theory focuses on preventing harm caused by reliance on an agreement.
An economic theory says contracts help people make useful exchanges and plans.
A relationship theory highlights cooperation and the special connection between the people who contract.
Some philosophers think no single theory explains every contract rule.
summaries.why_it_matters: Contracts shape everyday activities such as buying things, hiring people, borrowing money, and making plans. Understanding the competing theories helps us ask what fairness requires when an agreement is unclear, broken, or made under pressure. It also shows that a legal rule can have several possible purposes, and that choosing among those purposes affects real people’s opportunities and responsibilities.

important_terms.definition: An agreement that the law recognizes and may enforce.
A serious commitment to do something for another person.
A choice made freely, with enough understanding and without unfair pressure.
Money meant to make up for what someone expected to gain from a broken contract.
The idea that a contract may serve several important goals instead of just one.

questions_to_think_about: Should every promise be enforced by law, or only promises made as part of an exchange?
If breaking a deal does not hurt anyone, is it still wrong?
Is paying money a good substitute for doing what was promised?
Can an agreement be truly free if one person has much less power or information?
Why might contract law need more than one guiding idea?

summaries.example: Suppose a seller agrees to deliver a machine to a buyer for $10,000. Before delivery, another buyer offers $12,000. Under a familiar expectation-based remedy, the seller might deliver to the second buyer and pay the first buyer the value of the lost bargain, if that payment adequately covers the first buyer’s expectation. Supporters of an efficiency account may see this as moving the machine to its higher-valued use. Supporters of a promise-based account may see a serious conflict: the law appears to permit substitution of money for performance rather than requiring the promise to be kept.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of contract law studies the structure and justification of legal obligations that people voluntarily create through agreement. The source presents five broad approaches. The promise approach treats contract as a legal expression of promissory morality, but it must explain why the state should enforce promises for their own sake and why contract doctrine differs from ordinary morality. A harm-based approach grounds duties in misleading others, reasonable reliance, and the avoidance of harm, yet it has difficulty explaining expectation remedies and liability even without reliance. An economic approach sees contract law as a system that enables mutually beneficial exchange and investment; it explains some doctrines, including incentives for efficient breach, but faces objections about fairness, autonomy, mandatory rules, and the limits of judicial lawmaking. Relational approaches ground contractual obligation in cooperation, reciprocity, recognition, or the exchange of rights, while confronting the question of whether legal incentives crowd out richer social motives. Pluralism holds that contract law may embody several partly conflicting values. The entry also examines interpretation, freedom, intention in standard forms, and distributive justice.
key_ideas: The central theories differ over whether contracts enforce promises, prevent harm, promote welfare, express a special relationship, or combine several aims.
Expectation remedies support the promisee’s anticipated value, while reliance remedies focus on losses caused by reliance; this difference creates theoretical pressure.
An efficiency theory can explain why the law may tolerate some breaches, but it faces questions about penalties, mandatory rules, fairness, and judicial authority.
Relational theories understand contracting as cooperation or reciprocal recognition, yet must explain contracts between organizations and self-interested parties.
Contract law treats freedom as important, but fraud, duress, incapacity, information problems, and unequal bargaining power complicate the idea of voluntary agreement.
Modern standard-form contracts raise a problem for theories that rely on conscious promising or clearly formed intentions.
summaries.why_it_matters: Contracts are not merely private promises; they are legal institutions that organize economic and social cooperation. Their rules decide when speech creates obligations, how ambiguity is handled, what counts as free consent, and what follows from breach. The competing theories clarify why apparently technical questions—such as damages, disclosure, or standard-form terms—also involve moral questions about trust, welfare, authority, freedom, and equality.

important_terms.definition: A legal obligation created through a person’s voluntary agreement or other legally recognized act.
The moral view that contract law chiefly enforces duties created by promises.
A legal remedy designed to place the injured party near the position they would have occupied if the contract had been performed.
A remedy that reimburses losses caused by relying on an agreement, rather than awarding the full expected gain.
The view that contract rules should promote beneficial exchange, investment, or overall welfare.
The normative status or significance created by the contractual relationship itself.
The view that several values or purposes may guide contract law, without one master principle.
The ability to choose with adequate understanding and without coercion or wrongful pressure.

questions_to_think_about: Does a legal system have sufficient justification to enforce promises simply because keeping promises is morally valuable?
If expectation damages make breach attractive when performance is costly, is the resulting breach wrong, efficient, or both?
Can a promise-based theory explain consideration, which generally limits enforcement to bargains?
What makes consent meaningful when a person clicks agreement without reading a standard form?
Should contract law directly reduce inequality, or should redistribution mainly occur through broader political institutions?

summaries.example: A student-run snack club orders 100 granola bars from a supplier for a school event. The supplier later sells them elsewhere because another buyer offers more. The club expected to earn money from the sale. One philosopher might say the supplier must respect a promise. Another might focus on the club’s planning and possible losses. An economist might ask whether paying the club for its expected gain lets the bars go to the buyer who values them most. A different view might ask what cooperation and fair dealing between the two sides require.
summaries.summary: Contracts are agreements that the law uses to give people control over some of their future duties and rights. The source asks what makes this legal system justified. The promise view says the law should protect commitments. The harm-based view says that people should not create serious, reasonable expectations and then leave others to bear the resulting harm. The economic view says enforceable agreements help people plan, invest, and make exchanges that produce mutual gains. Relational views focus on cooperation and the special position each contracting party gives the other. Pluralism combines these possibilities by saying that contract law may serve several goals that do not always fit neatly together. The entry also discusses difficult cases involving unclear language, pressure, unequal information, and standard online forms. It asks whether contract law should mainly enforce choices people made, improve social welfare, protect relationships, or address unfair distributions.
key_ideas: Contract law gives people a way to shape their future legal rights and duties.
The promise theory emphasizes fidelity: agreements matter because people commit themselves.
The harm theory emphasizes assurances, reliance, and the risk of leaving others worse off.
The economic theory emphasizes cooperation, investment, and gains from trade, even if a party sometimes breaches and pays damages.
Relational theories see contracts as forms of cooperation in which each side recognizes the other’s authority or interests.
Contract rules can protect freedom and fairness, but philosophers disagree about how much they should correct unequal bargaining power.
summaries.why_it_matters: Most people encounter contracts through purchases, jobs, subscriptions, services, and online forms. Philosophical theories help explain why some agreements are enforced, why some can be cancelled, and why a broken agreement may lead to money rather than forced performance. They also reveal that decisions about contracts involve larger questions: How free must a choice be? How much should law care about inequality? And can different values be balanced in one legal system?

important_terms.definition: A deal recognized by law, creating duties for the people who make it.
A commitment that can give another person a reason to expect a certain action.
The value a person expected to receive if the agreement had been carried out.
Losses caused by acting in reliance on what someone agreed to do.
A rule or idea that helps people coordinate their actions and gain from working together.
The special importance or force of a relationship created by an agreement.
An approach saying contract law has several important purposes rather than one single purpose.
The ability to make an informed choice without force, deception, or unfair control.

questions_to_think_about: Is breaking a contract wrong even when the other person did not rely on it?
When is paying damages an acceptable alternative to carrying out an agreement?
What makes an offer different from a threat when both influence someone’s choice?
Should a court look only at the written words, or also at the surrounding conversation?
Can one set of contract rules promote both efficiency and fairness?
